name: The Wisdom Literature and Psalms: Writings (Ketuvim)

objectives.text: Identify the Psalms as songs and prayers that God's people sang to worship him
Recite Psalm 23:1-3 and describe how the Lord cares for his people like a shepherd cares for sheep
Identify Solomon as the king who asked God for wisdom and wrote many proverbs
Identify David as the shepherd king who wrote many of the psalms
Name in order the poetic and wisdom books of the Old Testament: Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and Song of Songs
Explain from Proverbs that the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom
Describe how creation declares the glory of God using Psalm 19
Identify the different emotions the psalmists express, such as joy, sorrow, fear, and trust, and explain that the psalms show God's people bringing every situation to him in prayer
Retell the story of Job's testing, his response, and God's restoration of him
Explain the difference between a proverb as a general principle of wise living and a promise from God
Contrast the way of the righteous and the way of the wicked as presented in Psalm 1
Compare Job's questioning in suffering with the expressions of trust in God found in the Psalms
Summarize the message of Ecclesiastes about life under the sun and its concluding call to fear God and keep his commandments
Describe the arrangement of the Psalter into five books, each closing with a doxology
Analyze examples of Hebrew parallelism, distinguishing synonymous, antithetical, and synthetic lines
Analyze the figurative language and structures of Hebrew poetry, including metaphor and acrostic form
Explain the Reformed practice of singing psalms in worship and sing a metrical psalm in class
Identify the Writings as the third division of the Hebrew Bible alongside the Law and the Prophets, as Jesus referred to it
Analyze God's speeches to Job and explain what they teach about God's sovereign providence and the limits of human understanding
Explain how Jesus prayed and quoted the Psalms during his ministry and on the cross
Compose an original lament or praise psalm that follows the structure and parallelism of biblical examples
Analyze the meaning of the Hebrew word hebel, often translated vanity or vapor, across Ecclesiastes and explain how it supports the book's conclusion
Explain how the Song of Songs celebrates covenant love in marriage and how the church has also read it in light of Christ and his church
Classify psalms by genre, including lament, hymn of praise, thanksgiving, royal, and wisdom psalms, and identify the typical structure of each
Explain how the New Testament applies royal and messianic psalms to Christ as prophet, priest, and king
Analyze the personification of Wisdom in Proverbs 8 and how the New Testament presents Christ as the wisdom of God
Evaluate how Job, the Psalms, and Ecclesiastes challenge a simple view that suffering always results from personal sin
Evaluate the counsel of Proverbs on speech, work, money, and friendship and apply it to contemporary situations
Analyze the imprecatory psalms in their context and explain how they entrust judgment to God in light of New Testament teaching
Write a synthesis essay showing how the Wisdom books and Psalms point to Christ as the fulfillment of the pursuit of wisdom

changes: Kept and reworded the real competencies (Psalms as songs, Solomon, Psalm 23, fear of the Lord, proverb vs promise, Job vs Psalms, Ecclesiastes, parallelism, Job and providence, Jesus and the Psalms, hebel, psalm genres, suffering, practical Proverbs, wisdom in Christ). Dropped the vague 'observe poetry and feelings' objective and replaced it with text-based analysis of the psalmists' expressions. Added David as psalmist, naming the books, Psalm 19 and creation, the two ways of Psalm 1, the five books of the Psalter, poetic devices, Reformed psalm singing, the Writings in the Hebrew canon, composing a psalm, Song of Songs, messianic psalms, Wisdom personified in Proverbs 8, and imprecatory psalms. Anchored all objectives to specific verses and added confession references where they state the doctrine. Left Ruth, Esther, Chronicles, Lamentations, and Daniel to the historical and prophetic sibling sub-topics.
